stories.title: World leaders gather for United Nations General Assembly
stories.summary: The United Nations General Assembly's high-level general debate begins today. Nearly 130 heads of state and government, and other high-level representatives are to meet with their counterparts and address the assembly with their national statements over the next three days. Taoiseach Micheál Martin is due to participate in several bilateral meetings and attend a number of engagements relating to developments in the Middle East, including a meeting of the 'Global Alliance for the Implementation of the Two-State Solution’. The group's aims are to work towards a two-state solution and support efforts to reach a permanent ceasefire in Gaza. The Taoiseach is also expected to participate in an event hosted by French President Emmanuel Macron, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, to mark nearly a year since the Gaza peace plan was announced. Meetings between Mr Martin and outgoing UN Secretary General António Guterres, New York Governor Kathy Hochul and Mayor Zohran Mamdani have also been scheduled.

stories.title: Man dies after collision between car and bus in Waterford
stories.summary: A man in his 60s has died following a collision involving a car and a bus in Co Waterford yesterday evening. The collision occurred at around 8pm on the N25 between Youghal and Dungarvan at Kinsalebeg. The bus driver and passengers were assessed at the scene and no serious injuries were reported. Bus Éireann said that the bus was one of its Expressway vehicles, serving the Cork-Waterford route (40), and that it was supporting gardaí in their investigation of the incident. The road was closed for a technical examination but has since reopened. Gardaí are appealing for any witnesses, particularly anyone travelling on the N25 between Grange and Pilltown Cross between 7.30pm and 8pm last night and who may have camera footage (including dash-cam) is asked to contact Dungarvan Garda Station on 058 48600, the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111, or any garda station.

stories.title: Calls for Govt to reject proposed minimum wage increase
stories.summary: The Small Firms Association has called on the Government to reject the proposed increase in the national minimum wage in the forthcoming budget to help small businesses cope with rising labour-related costs. In its pre-budget submission, the SFA said there is a critical need to halt further wage hikes proposed by the Low Pay Commission to ensure the survival of viable enterprises. In July, it was reported that the Low Pay Commission had recommended that the minimum wage should increase by 5.6%. If the proposals are accepted by the Government, it would see the rate rise by 79 cent an hour from €14.15 to €14.94. In its submission, the SFA said that the minimum wage has moved from €9.15 in 2016 to €14.15 in 2026. "While the national minimum wage increased by 54.6% in the same period, the Consumer Price Index (CPI) increased by roughly 25% cumulatively from 2016 to 2026," according to the SFA.

stories.title: AMD joins $1 trillion club as chipmakers rally
stories.summary: Advanced Micro Devices soared past $1 trillion in market capitalisation for the first time last night, joining a small group of chipmakers to reach the milestone, as investors bet on its expanding role in AI computing. AMD shares were last up 9.6% at $613.31, scaling a record high. The milestone caps a stellar rally for the California-based company, regarded as the closest rival to AI bellwether Nvidia for graphics processing units. It becomes only the fourth US chipmaker to top a $1 trillion valuation, after Nvidia, Broadcom and Micron. Nvidia crossed the mark in 2023 and is now the world's most valuable company, worth more than $5 trillion. "Money is moving back into the AI trade," said Thomas Hayes, chairman at Great Hill Capital LLC in New York. Enthusiasm for chipmakers cooled in recent months as markets scrutinised AI spending by hyperscalers. Higher oil prices linked to the US-Iran conflict and expectations of higher-for-longer interest rates added to the pressure. But now investors believe AI is the only area that can work in a Federal Reserve-induced economic slowdown, Hayes said. "AMD is representative of that."

stories.title: More than 1.6m urged to evacuate as typhoon nears Tokyo
stories.summary: Hundreds of flights were cancelled and more than one million people were under evacuation advisories in Japan as Typhoon Dujuan approached Tokyo, potentially bringing record rainfall. Japan often sees strong typhoons in the late summer and early autumn, and other storms have already disrupted some events at the Asian Games being hosted in the country. Dujuan was bringing winds of around 144 kilometres per hour as it moved to around 130 kilometres south of Katsuura City near Tokyo. Japan Airlines cancelled 135 flights and All Nippon Airways scrapped 140, while more than 9,000 households near Tokyo were without power. More than 1.6 million residents in and around the capital were urged to evacuate, according to the Fire and Disaster Management Agency. Landslide warnings were issued for Tokyo as well as for Chiba, Kanagawa and Shizuoka prefectures. Railway operators in Tokyo and neighbouring regions suspended services on some lines.

stories.title: Flying jockey Flanagan keeping busy on Listowel week
stories.summary: The Harvest Festival in Listowel kicked off in earnest over the weekend but for jockey, valet and pilot Sean Flanagan, he was busier than most. The Wexford man had a big win on the opening day of the festival as a jockey, taking the Kinisla Handicap Steeplechase aboard Net Boy, but he's been busy transporting his fellow jockeys from the course and to other courses as well. Come Monday, his pilot licence came in handy as he helped Sam Coen ride horses in Listowel and then in Fairyhouse. "There's not many mixed, double meetings here anymore", Flanagan explained. "The odd lad had tried to do both and obviously Listowel to Fairyhouse is geologically, not very workable, but with the valeting team we look after some of the lads and they just rang up and asked would I be able to do them a turn and I enjoy a bit of flying and sure it's grand." That noble act to some was just a normal day for Flanagan who even had time to enjoy the surrounds in his aeroplane on a calm and clear Monday.

stories.title: Rathmore deny Dr Crokes the three-in-a-row in Kerry
stories.summary: Rathmore are Kerry Senior Club champions for the first time since 2011, a victory made all the sweeter for beating their East Kerry rivals, Dr Crokes, and denying the Killarney club a three-in-a-row of titles. Dr Crokes will reflect on a barrowload of wides and missed shots, and the first half dismissal of Micheal Burns for shoving a physio to the ground as obvious reasons for them relinquishing their title, but there was no denying Rathmore a first title in 15 years, with a goal in either half just about underscoring their superiority. Their first goal was the game's first score, Fionn Murphy slipping his short low shot past Shane Murphy in the 11th minute, with Ciaran Collins adding a point a minute later. Dr Crokes responded with a Tony Brosnan point and a two-pointer from Micheal Burns, but things went from orange to red for Burns a couple of minutes later. An off-the-ball scuffle between Mark O’Shea and Collins saw Cathal Ryan intervene at the expense of a black card, but it was Burns’s shove on the Rathmore physio attending to Collins that saw the Dr Crokes man dismissed, and the medic being shown a yellow card. When order was restored, Brosnan kicked a pair of points for the champions, with Darragh Nagle and Collins replying in kind for Dr Crokes, who trailed 0-06 to 1-04 at half time. Brendan O’Keeffe’s two-pointer early in the second half extended Rathmore’s lead, but Dr Crokes proved tough to shake off, with their accuracy improving somewhat in the second period, though Brosnan fluffed a gilt-edged chance from the penalty spot as he lifted his shot over the crossbar after Evan Looney had been taken down in the square.

stories.title: Palmer and Rice among five ruled out of England squad
stories.summary: Five England players, including Chelsea forward Cole Palmer, have dropped out of the squad for the Nations League matches over the next three weeks. Arsenal midfielder Declan Rice, Newcastle full-back Tino Livramento and the Manchester United pair of Marcus Rashford and Kobbie Mainoo complete the quintet who have been declared unavailable due to injury, with Everton's James Garner and Nottingham Forest’s Morgan Gibbs-White drafted in. England take on world champions Spain on 26 September before a trip to face Czechia on 29 September. They are away to Croatia on 3 October before completing the international break with a home clash with Czechia on 6 October. Garner and Gibbs-White will join the rest of the squad in reporting to St George’s Park on Tuesday, the Football Association said in an update on Monday afternoon. Palmer had been set to make a return to the England fold after being omitted from Thomas Tuchel's World Cup squad, and played the full match as Chelsea lost to Brentford on Friday. The FA did not disclose any specifics regarding the player injuries. Livramento was unable to feature for Newcastle in their win over Hull on Saturday, while Rashford and Mainoo were substituted before the end of their side’s draw at Fulham on Sunday.

stories.title: USA defeat doesn't dampen debut feeling for Adams Verling
stories.summary: A 40-36 defeat to the USA means it won't go down as a dream debut for Ireland’s latest international Jemima Adams Verling, but the Connacht back row insists her first cap is still "the most incredible experience" of her life. The 20-year-old played 50 minutes on debut at Tallaght Stadium yesterday and looked at home in Test rugby, logging a whopping 16 tackles in just 50 minutes on the pitch. Ireland were 31-12 in front and seemingly cruising against Jack Hanratty’s side when Adams Verling was replaced by Brittany Hogan with 30 minutes to play. But even the second half collapse did little to quench her enthusiasm as she reflected on her first cap. "It's always unfortunate to come out with a loss at the back of the game but it was just the most incredible experience of my life and I've just so much pride for the girls," Adams Verling said. "They put their hearts out there and the intent I saw from all of them, even when I came off, they were absolutely impeccable.

stories.title: 5 must-see shows at this year's Dublin Theatre Festival
stories.summary: We asked Dublin Theatre Festival Artistic Director Róise Goan to pick her 5 must-sees from the 2026 edition of DTF, which runs from 24 September to 11 October. We have to start with our opening show, Radio Bette. The Goat Exchange are the hottest theatre company in New York right now, named as New York Times Critics Picks twice in the last 9 months. This production brings together amazing stars of TV and Broadway like Michael Cerveris and Roberta Colindrez to revisit the career of Bette Davis and in particular the iconic classic All About Eve. Expect backstage drama, extreme glamour, Hollywood nostalgia with a contemporary New York edge. Even if you don't know and love All About Eve, If you liked GATZ at Dublin Theatre Festival many moons ago, or if you enjoyed Blue Moon or Sentimental Value at the cinema in the last year, you will love this. Brokentalkers are a brilliant theatre company, who shine a light on some of the most urgent questions of our time, with empathy and humour. In Heroes Of Tomorrow, they tackle the moral responsibility of artists in the a world where truth itself is contested. If you’ve been following the Ed Sheeran/Macklemore/Pink debacle, or if you’ve read Careless People and are keen to think about big moral conundrums, while also being entertained with a witty and thoughtful script, this one is for you. Dead Centre, the brilliant Irish theatre company behind Deaf Republic, Good Sex, and many other Dublin Theatre Festival hits, return with this brilliant show about a man whose nationality changed 5 times throughout his life because of shifting borders and the pressure on natural resources. You will definitely learn something new about European history you didn’t know, but as ever with Dead Centre, the narrative will twist and turn in exciting ways and you’ll have a great time while it’s happening. The kind of show that you want a talk about over a pint/dinner immediately! Last year we had the great fortune to welcome Rebecca Chaillon to the festival with her excellent show Whitewashing, which wowed audiences. She returns with an even bigger show, exploring the search for hope at a challenging time for the planet, with great humour, audacity and BUTTER. It’s big, it’s messy, it’s often hilarious. It’s utterly original and gives an excellent portrait of life right now from a young, queer, fat, black and working class French perspective. If you’ve a habit of doomscrolling way past your bedtime, and you need a fresh take, this is well worth your time. Xnthony makes his festival debut with this cracker of a new musical. Looking at a crisis in faith across generations, he pays homage to those in need of faith and looking for a cure, while perfectly capturing the kitsch magic of a pilgrimage to Lourdes. stories.summary: Sense and Sensibility stars Daisy Edgar-Jones and Caitríona Balfe believe audiences will relate to the Dashwoods' financial insecurities, and hope viewers come away from the new adaptation with a renewed appreciation for the strength and resilience of women. The film, directed by Georgia Oakley and written by Diana Reid, is a reimagining of Jane Austen’s much-loved classic novel of the same name. Daisy Edgar-Jones plays Elinor Dashwood, while Caitríona Balfe stars as Mrs Dashwood, the mother of Elinor and Marianne (Esmé Creed-Miles) and Margaret (Bodhi Rae Breathnach). "I think the true love story is between the women and the sisters and the Dashwood family, definitely. "They go through a lot at the beginning of the film. They lose their fortune and, at that time especially, it was very difficult to be a woman and to survive, and they really come together. There’s such a strength between them," she explained. For Monaghan woman Balfe, the relationship between the sisters was also an important part of the story, particularly given her own household growing up.

stories.title: Maura Derrane on bold fashion statements and working with Dáithí
stories.summary: As she returns to the Today show for a 15th season, Maura Derrane tells Clare O'Mahony why she thinks the show chimes with its viewers, how her innate curiosity makes it her natural media home and getting evil with Dáithí Ó Sé just before they go on air, "Everywhere I go in Ireland, and even away, if you meet an Irish person, they’re like, 'When are you back to the show?’," says Maura Derrane. "It’s become a staple, and I think that’s so brilliant." She says she had just such queries recently while shopping, as one person after another asked when Today would be returning after its summer break. 14 years on air, the programme is woven into the rhythm of its viewers’ lives, ending as the summer begins and returning as children settle back into school. "It’s a kind of home from home in Cork, and a lot of the people I work with have been there since the beginning. There’s a real family feeling because we’re not a big team, but we’ve been together for a long time." The summer break gave Maura time for trips to Italy and Portugal, although much of her summer was spent at home on Inis Mór. Her mother Bridgie is now 90, and those weeks allow Maura to make up for time away during the working year. She says that Cal, who has a cousin a few years older there, loves the island too. Going home also means returning to the garden and food she grew up with. Her family has always grown potatoes and vegetables in a centuries-old way, using seaweed gathered on the island’s shore, while her sister Barbara, who is also an artist, now grows grapes in a polytunnel. "She’s totally exotic down there," Maura laughs. "She’s like Tahiti-slash-Inis Mór!"
stories.rssSummary: "I feel it is my duty for the Irish people to push myself a little bit," she says. "Sometimes it's good to give yourself a kick up the ass fashion-wise."

stories.summary: The number of legal aid certificates granted in July this year fell by 93% compared to last year, according to the Law Society, which will appear before the Oireachtas Committee on Justice later today. A new Criminal Legal Aid Scheme was introduced in July this year by Minister for Justice Jim O'Callaghan, which replaced a per-appearance fee with a €520 flat rate, prompting hundreds of solicitors to withdraw their services. In its opening statement to the committee, the Law Society will say the new scheme is having a real and negative impact on how the legal aid system operates. It will say the number of legal aid certificates granted collapsed to just 702, compared to July 2025 when 10,277 such certificates were issued. Law Society President Rosemarie Loftus is expected to tell the committee that a fall of this scale is deeply worrying and has been reflected in courts across the country. She will say that the effectiveness of the constitutional right to legal representation is threatened by the current situation, as the State is required to provide legal representation to those who cannot afford it.

stories.title: Judges warned of 'significant' disruption to courts
stories.summary: Senior judges have been warned there is likely to be "significant" disruption to court proceedings amid the ongoing criminal legal aid dispute. It is understood that dozens of solicitors have outlined their concerns in letters to the Chief Justice and the presidents of the High Court, Circuit Court, and District Court. In one letter seen by the Press Association, a solicitor engaged in the withdrawal of services tells the senior judges that the dispute with the Department of Justice has "not been resolved at this point". Tony Collier, of Ferrys Solicitors, says they will not be in a position to provide criminal defence services under the new legal aid model except for limited circumstances. In advance of the return of higher courts in October, Mr Collier says that solicitors have made an "enormous effort" to resolve the dispute but claims Minister for Justice Jim O'Callaghan has "failed to engage in any meaningful way". The letter says that the minister is awaiting a judgment in judicial review matters relating to the dispute, describing the position as "unfortunate".

stories.title: New AI Office to develop trust in the technology - Burke
stories.summary: The State's new AI Office will play a key role in developing public trust in the technology, according to Minister for Enterprise Peter Burke. Oifig Intleacht Shaorga na hÉireann - the AI Office of Ireland - is based in the Department of Enterprise, but it is fully independent. The Cabinet heard today that Paul Byrne is the new Chief Executive of the Office. It is tasked with ensuring that Ireland meets its obligations under the EU AI Act as well as carrying out its own research. Mr Burke told colleagues that establishing the Office quickly was a priority given the rapidly increasing significance of AI adoption. Mr Byrne previously worked for the Medical Council of Ireland, where he served as Executive Director of Education, Innovation and Artificial Intelligence.

stories.title: Oil prices climb ahead of potential US-Iran talks
stories.summary: Oil prices gained today after declining for four consecutive sessions as investors awaited developments on potential US-Iran talks at the United Nations General Assembly this week after more supplies emerged through the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend. The Brent crude futures November contract rose $1.29, or 1.29%, to $101.63 a barrel this morning. The WTI October contract, which expires today, climbed 92 cents, or 0.96%, to $96.70 a barrel. The more actively traded November contract was up 80 cents, or 0.87%, at $93.17 a barrel. Tehran and Washington exchanged threats on Sunday, though US President Donald Trump said he would be open to meeting Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who is expected to be in New York this week for the UN meeting. The rebound in crude suggests traders need fresh developments on supply risks or diplomatic efforts before pushing prices materially lower, said Ole Hansen, head of commodity strategy at Saxo Bank. Over the weekend, Iran also conveyed its conditions to mediators for re-engaging in negotiations, Al Jazeera reported, citing Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei.

stories.title: Putin's party wins record majority in Russian election
stories.summary: Vladimir Putin's ruling United Russia party has won a record majority in the country's parliamentary elections, marked by cyberattacks and a barrage of Ukrainian drone strikes. United Russia won a record 355 seats in Russia's 450-seat Duma lower house of parliament, according to preliminary results from the three-day election released by electoral chief Ella Pamfilova today. With almost all votes counted from the poll, in which no parties critical of Mr Putin took part, results showed the presidential party will have a supermajority, larger than its previous 2016 record of 343 seats. It was Russia's first parliamentary election since Moscow launched its Ukraine offensive in 2022. The Kremlin tightly controls elections and Moscow has banned criticism of its military campaign in Ukraine. Ms Pamfilova said turnout was more than 59%, thanking Russians for voting despite what she called "psychological pressure" on the country.

stories.title: Lancaster eyes on Connacht extension rather than Leinster
stories.summary: Stuart Lancaster said he is in talks with Connacht about extending his contract and that there has been no contact with Leinster about taking over there when Leo Cullen departs at the end of the season. Lancaster spent seven seasons as senior coach under Cullen at Leinster and was immediately identified in many quarters as a possible successor when Cullen announced his intention in June to leave at the end of this campaign. But Lancaster, who signed a two-year deal when he arrived in Connacht last summer, said there has been no contact with Leinster and that he, in fact, is in talks with Connacht CEO Willie Ruane and IRFU performance director David Humphreys. "Honestly, I've not had any conversation with anyone from Leinster," said Lancaster as he prepares for Friday night's URC opener against the Stormers in Galway. "Either them ringing me or me ringing them. So, no, there's no communication there." Lancaster and his wife Nina have settled well in Galway and on the field he made a huge impact in his first season, with Connacht winning seven of their last eight URC games to secure a knockout place in the league and a spot in this season’s Champions Cup when they will face four previous winners in Toulouse, Saracens, Exeter and Ronan O’Gara’s La Rochelle.

stories.title: Leitrim's Casey ready for more after faithfulness tested
stories.summary: No word of a lie, Donal Casey's life has changed utterly in the past 12 months. A year ago this weekend, the then 23-year-old was in game mode, an interested spectator in the crowd as the Leitrim SFC quarter-finals were playing out. Nothing really mattered at that time apart from a manic determination to help Leitrim Gaels, who had safely navigated a path to the semi-finals, get their hands on the Fenagh Perpetual Cup for the first time in the club’s history. Life's most valuable information in that moment was finding out who would be facing Mal Guckian’s side in the last four. He did help his club to that coveted silverware, but life isn’t just about football anymore. After what happened in that county final, his outlook changed forever. Back to that 2025 county final though and the victory over Sean O’Heslin’s. It was a day when dreams should have been realised, but for the young centre half-back, it came so close to complete tragedy.

stories.title: Former Ireland international Jack McDonagh dies aged 64
stories.summary: Former Ireland international centre half Jack 'Jacko' McDonagh has passed away at the age of 64, his former club Shamrock Rovers announced on Monday. McDonagh played three times at senior level for the Republic of Ireland under the managership of Eoin Hand across 1983 and 1984, having had a stellar career domestically and a brief stint in France and Belgium. Hailing from Donnybrook originally, McDonagh started his career with the Shelbourne youths before making the switch to Bohemians. During this spell, he won the PFAI Young Player of the Year for the 1981-82 season. He played 60 times across three seasons with the Gypsies before making the switch south to Rovers. McDonagh played on the four-in-a-row team in 1983/84 and 1984/85, the latter season having won the league and FAI Cup double. Also in 1983, he would make his Ireland debut under Hand, as they defeated Malta 8-0 in Dalymount Park.

stories.title: Ireland throw away 19-point lead in defeat to USA
stories.summary: Ireland threw away a 19-point lead to lose to the United States 36-40 in Tallaght in their opening game of the WXV Global Series. Scott Bemand's side stormed to a 17-0 lead in the first 20 minutes with the United States looking like they had little response. Ireland's opener came after Stacey Flood made a brilliant line break to feed Vicky Elmes Kinlan on the left wing for a try that looked like it was made on the training field. Dannah O'Brien pulled the subsequent conversion to the left and wide. Ireland's lineout, which left a lot to be desired in the second half, was a fruitful tool in the first and Cliodhna McDonald Moloney made her presence known when she bashed over the line from the back of the maul after 14 minutes. She was to be back in action just four minutes later as she found herself inches from the tryline but just not able to get it across. With a number of people on her shoulder, she opted to pass the ball to Aoife Wafer who took it over the line. O'Brien converted the third time of asking and it looked like Ireland were going into cruise control.

stories.title: U2 at 50: The 10 best U2 songs of all time, ranked
stories.summary: Freelance journalist and broadcaster, writing about music and the arts. Happy Birthday, U2! One of the biggest rock bands of all time celebrates 50 years in business this month, with 15 studio albums, 12 EPs, three compilations, two live albums and no less than 85 singles released by the Dublin band over the course of that half-century. The question is, which songs are their best? It may be overplayed, it may be somewhat overcooked, it may not have the emotional heft of some of their other tracks - but only a curmudgeon would argue against Beautiful Day being one of U2’s most euphoric songs. Taken from 2001’s pivotal All That You Can’t Leave Behind album, it ushered in a new era for the band while cementing their position as one of the finest stadium rock bands on the planet. That intro alone is worth its weight in gold: the yearning squeal of The Edge’s guitar, the piano riff, the tremulous bassline, that primitive yowl of Bono’s…. 43 years after it was first released, New Year’s Day sounds as fresh as ever. The first track from U2’s third album War also incorporated social and political themes, written about the revolutionary Polish solidarity movement in 1980 which eventually led to the collapse of communism in Poland. Apparently it was originally intended as a love song about Ali Hewson. No harm, no foul, Ali. U2 have always looked to the wider world for inspiration, but this song - also taken from War - brought them closer to home and is perhaps their most explicitly political song to date. Written about the Troubles and specifically the Bloody Sunday atrocity of 1972, it’s a protest song about the futility of war, wrapped up in a spiky rock tune. From Larry Mullen’s martial cadence to Bono’s exasperated lyrics ("How long, how long must we sing this song?"), it still packs a mighty punch. By 1987, U2 had spent much of the decade touring extensively in America and absorbing its culture from the inside looking out. The result was The Joshua Tree - the album that many fans still consider their defining moment. The swarthy shuck of the guitar riff on this song, coupled with the gospel undertones and Bono’s preacher-like lyrics as it slips into the deep groove of Adam Clayton’s bassline is simply sensational stuff.

stories.title: Taylor Swift to make VMAs history with director honour
stories.summary: Taylor Swift is set to become the most-awarded artist in MTV Video Music Awards history after being named the first recipient of a new honour recognising musicians for their work behind the camera. CBS and MTV have announced that Swift will receive the inaugural MTV VMA Artist Director Honours at this year's ceremony in Los Angeles on Sunday. The new award recognises artists whose directing work has helped advance music video and visual storytelling. The honour will take Swift’s VMA tally to 31, moving her ahead of Beyoncé. The pair are currently tied as the most-awarded musicians in VMA history, with 30 awards each. Swift is a seven-time nominee and four-time winner in the VMAs’ Best Direction category. Her directing work includes videos and films such as The Fate of Ophelia, Opalite, The Man, All Too Well: The Short Film, Anti-Hero, Bejeweled and Fortnight.

stories.title: 5 ways the transition into autumn can impact your sleep
stories.summary: The transition from summer to autumn can sometimes be tricky to navigate, as the dramatic change in weather and reduction of sunlight can often have both subtle and significant impacts on our sleep schedule. We spoke to some sleep experts who explained five key ways autumn can change your sleep, and offered helpful recommendations on how to adapt to this. 1. Temperature change can impact the time it takes to fall asleep "We often have a lot of fluctuations in temperature this time of year, which can have an impact on people’s comfort before bed," says James Wilson, also known as ‘The Sleep Geek’, resident sleep expert at Bensons For Beds. Temperature plays an important part in the falling asleep process. "In order to fall asleep, our body wants to reduce its internal body temperature by around one degree. Therefore, compared to summer, cooler temperatures in autumn can benefit our sleep because it tends to be easier to get rid of your internal heat and fall asleep quicker," explains Dr Kat Lederle, sleep and circadian rhythm specialist at The London General Practice.

stories.title: 7 in 10 young adults considering leaving Ireland - survey
stories.summary: Almost seven in ten young adults are considering moving abroad for a better quality of life, according to new research from the National Youth Council of Ireland (NYCI). The survey found that 68% of 18-24 year olds are considering moving abroad, while 71% believe they would have a better quality of life outside Ireland. Housing and affordability remain the main concerns, but worries about employment have increased year on year. Nine in ten young adults said it is becoming harder to find secure, well-paid work. A similar proportion said they had been negatively affected by the cost of living, while 89% agreed that the housing crisis disproportionately affects young people. Transport costs and mental health also remain prominent concerns.

stories.title: EU urged to act faster on online risks facing children
stories.summary: Stronger regulation is needed to protect children from online abuse, exploitation and unsafe platforms, the Online Safety Coordinator with the Children's Rights Alliance has urged. Noeline Blackwell's comments come after the European Commission proposed a ban on social media access for children under 13, alongside new "safe design" obligations for platforms used by young people aged 15 to 18. In her State of the Union address last week, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said it was "time for Europe to act", outlining plans for a new Kids Act that would take a "gradual and differentiated approach" to protecting children online. Under the proposals, children under 13 would be barred from accessing social media platforms. "They have been gathering evidence over time," she said, citing a report published in July that identified addictive platform features which can be harmful to children when used excessively. She said the commission's evidence-led approach shifts responsibility back to technology companies to ensure their products are safe.

stories.title: Govt may introduce tax break for childminders - Harris
stories.summary: Minister for Finance and Tánaiste Simon Harris has said the Government may introduce a tax break for childminders in next month's Budget. Speaking at the end of an informal gathering of EU Finance Ministers at Dublin Castle, Mr Harris confirmed he was considering the measure as the Coalition moves to finalise the specifics of Budget 2027 due to be announced on Tuesday fortnight. Senior Coalition figures have also indicated that a signalled reduction in the cost of home heating oil for householders will not be derived from a VAT cut despite the fuel industry advocating such a move. Mr Harris also reiterated his opposition to the abolition of stamp duty for first time buyers after the Taoiseach Micheál Martin last week said he had a "favourable disposition" towards the idea. Fianna Fáil Cork South Central TD Séamus McGrath has also pushed the move in recent weeks. Self-employed childminders in the home can currently earn up to €15,000 gross per year tax free.

stories.title: TUI narrows its operating profit outlook for 2026
stories.summary:
Germany's TUI narrowed its outlook for 2026 underlying operating earnings today, saying war in the Middle East meant customers were making later bookings, although demand was strong into the fourth quarter. Jet fuel prices have surged as a result of the disruption linked to the US-Israeli war on Iran and airlines have struggled to pass on increased costs, while customers are more hesitant about making travel plans. "Early indications for the new winter season point to a continuation of the later booking environment against the backdrop of ongoing geopolitical and economic uncertainty," the company said in a statement. Analysts pointed to increased forward bookings in recent weeks. Booked capacity for the core markets in Germany and Britain was up 1% since TUI's last results report on August 12, although overall reservations across segments were down compared to last year, according to the results. 

TUI, which runs cruise ships, airlines and hotels, cut its profit forecast and suspended its revenue guidance in March in response to the impact of the Iran war, which began at the end of February. The travel group expects annual underlying earnings before interest and taxes to reach between €1.2 billion and €1.3 billion, instead of the previously forecast €1.1 billion to €1.4 billion.

stories.title: Gaza health officials say Israeli fire kills three
stories.summary: Gaza health officials said Israeli fire killed three people, including a woman and a child, and injured several others across the Palestinian territory. Officials at Nasser hospital in the southern city of Khan Younis said the body of a child was brought to the medical facility after Israeli tanks opened fire on tents for displaced people in the Al-Mawasi area. Mahmoud Bassal, the spokesman for Gaza's civil defence agency, which operates as a rescue force under Hamas authority, said the child was 11 years old. In central Gaza, Al-Awda hospital officials said a 31-year-old woman died from her wounds after being shot by Israeli forces on Salah al-Din street east of Nuseirat refugee camp. Officials at Al-Shifa hospital in Gaza City said a man died after being shot in the head by a drone in Jabalia in northern Gaza. Gaza's civil defence said its teams had transported nine wounded people to hospitals following Israeli fire in Khan Yunis in the south and Bureij refugee camp in the centre of the territory.

stories.title: Kelly: Left-sided options a boost for Irish defence
stories.summary: The inclusion of uncapped defenders Liam Kitching and Joel Bagan offers Heimir Hallgrimsson more left-sided options, according to former Republic of Ireland international Stephen Kelly. The squad for Nations League matches against Kosovo, Israel and Austria included three players yet to make their respective international debuts. While Owen Elding is familiar to many from his League of Ireland days with Sligo Rovers and more recently with Hibernian in Scotland, Kitching and Bagan are more of an unknown quantity. Kitching caught the eye at Barnsley before securing a €5.25m move to Coventry City. He was a key fixture in Frank Lampard's side that achieved promotion to the Premier League last term, but the Sky Blues recruited heavily in defence and the 26-year-old found himself out of the first team. A season-long loan to Sheffield United has brought back regular football. Bagan was called into the squad for May's friendly against Grenada before pulling out with an injury.
